verses.translation_literal: In-beginning created God [obj] the-heavens and-[obj] the-earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the beginning, before any morning had a name, God created the heavens and the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a curtain line, not a lecture. Nobody is on stage but God, and the verb says so: bara', 'create', is used in the Bible only with God as its subject, so the actors have no human action to borrow from. Play it with total economy; seven Hebrew words, and the audience should feel the weight of every one.

How to take the first word is the oldest quarrel in the commentaries. The KJV's 'In the beginning God created' reads bereshit as absolute: a first act, creation from the start. Radak and Ramban read it so, Ramban adding that God began by creating the heavens and the earth from nothing and only afterwards their contents. Rashi, Rashbam and Ibn Ezra object that bereshit has no article and elsewhere stands in the construct, as in Jeremiah 26:1 and Hosea 1:2; they read 'In the beginning of God's creating the heavens and the earth', as YLT does. On that reading the verse is a time clause, and the main action begins with 'God said' in verse 3. The actor need not choose: the same seven words carry both, and the Hebrew consonants permit either.

The KJV also flattens 'the heavens' (shamayim, a plural form) into 'the heaven'. 'The heavens and the earth' is a merism, like 'day and night': Hebrew has no single word for 'universe', so it names the two poles and means everything. Elohim is a plural-form word taking a singular verb, which is how Hebrew writes the one God; 'God' here is not yet the covenant name YHWH.

philological_notes.note: 'In beginning'; from rosh, 'head'. It has no article. Rashi, Rashbam and Ibn Ezra take it as a construct ('in the beginning of God's creating', compare Jer 26:1 and Hos 1:2); Radak and Ramban take it as absolute ('at first, God created'). Both are grammatically possible.
'Created'. In the qal it has only God as subject in the Hebrew Bible and never names the material used. Ibn Ezra notes it can also mean 'cut, shape'.
A merism for the whole ordered cosmos. The object marker is repeated before 'the earth', making two equal objects.

verses.translation_literal: And-the-earth was formlessness and-emptiness, and-darkness [was] over [the] face-of [the] deep, and-[the] wind/spirit-of God [was] hovering over [the] face-of the-waters.
verses.translation_dramatic: The earth lay unshaped and empty, and darkness pressed on the face of the deep. Over the waters, in that silence, the Spirit of God hovered, trembling like wings over a nest.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three still pictures, then one movement. Darkness over the deep, formlessness on the land, and then the only moving thing in the frame: ruach elohim, hovering. Play the first half with held breath and the last word with a flutter.

The KJV's 'without form and void' is a fine echo of tohu wabohu, a rhyming pair that sounds like what it says: 'waste and wilderness', 'a formless nothing'. Radak glosses the pair as desolation and emptiness. Tohu elsewhere means desert wasteland (Deut 32:10); bohu occurs only in this phrase and in two prophets who quote it (Isa 34:11, Jer 4:23), where it means a land returned to chaos. The KJV's 'moved' is vague; merachefet is the verb of Deut 32:11, an eagle stirring over its young, and both Radak and Ibn Ezra cite that verse. And ruach can mean 'wind' as well as 'spirit': Radak offers both a divine will and a mighty wind, with 'of God' as an intensifier, as in 'a great city to God' (Jonah 3:3). The KJV chooses 'Spirit of God' and gives it a capital letter; the Hebrew gives no capitals.

Many scholars connect tehom, 'the deep', with Akkadian tiamtu and the sea-goddess Tiamat of Babylonian myth, and read the verse as a quiet polemic: here the deep is no goddess, only dark water with no will of its own. That is a modern proposal, not something the classical commentators in the packet say, and the Hebrew word itself is a plain common noun for deep water (Radak lists it as a feminine noun, with masculine uses in the Psalms).

philological_notes.note: A rhyming pair meaning 'formless waste and emptiness'. Tohu alone is the desert wasteland in Deut 32:10; bohu is found only in this pair and in Isa 34:11 and Jer 4:23.
'Hovering, fluttering'. Radak glosses it as 'stirring' and both he and Ibn Ezra compare Deut 32:11, an eagle over its young. The feminine participle fits ruach, a feminine noun.
'Spirit of God' or 'wind of God' (elohim possibly as superlative, 'mighty wind'). Radak gives both options. The layers read 'spirit' but the commentary names the alternative.
'The deep', the mass of water. Many scholars relate it to Akkadian tiamtu, 'sea', and the goddess Tiamat; this is a modern comparative proposal and the verse itself treats the deep as mere water.

verses.translation_literal: And-said God: Let-be light! And-was light.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God spoke into the dark: "Let there be light." And there was light.
verses.directors_commentary:
The shortest and most powerful beat in the scene: a command of two Hebrew words, yehi or, and its fulfillment of two more, vayehi or. Do not rush the gap, and do not decorate it; the point is that the word and the result are the same size and the same sound. The verb is a jussive, 'let it be', which in Hebrew is how a king gives an order, so God speaks here as sovereign, not as a craftsman working.

The KJV's 'Let there be light' is accurate and rightly famous. What it hides is the mirror: the command and its fulfillment are verbally identical, and only the 'and' in vayehi shows that the world has obeyed. Notice also that light comes before the sun, which is not created until day four: for the first audience, light is a gift of God, not a function of the sun gods of Egypt and Mesopotamia.

philological_notes.note: Jussive 'let there be light'. The fulfillment 'vayehi 'or' repeats the same words in the narrative tense, an exact echo.

verses.translation_literal: And-saw God [obj] the-light that [it was] good, and-separated God between the-light and-between the-darkness.
verses.translation_dramatic: God looked at the light and saw that it was good. Then he drew a line between the light and the darkness, and held each in its place.
verses.directors_commentary:
God is now an observer, and the first judgment in the Bible is a verdict on a thing seen. Tov, 'good', here means fit for its purpose, working, as a tool is good. Let the actor look before he speaks.

The verb vayavdel, 'separated', begins a thread that runs through the chapter (also in 1:6, 7, 14, 18) and it is the central act of the whole creation account: making by dividing. The KJV's 'divided' is fair, but it reads 'between the light and the darkness' as if the darkness had been abolished. It has not: the darkness is separated, kept, and in the next verse given a name. Note that Hebrew says 'between' twice ('between the light and between the darkness'), which gives the sentence a swinging, balanced shape.

philological_notes.note: 'And he separated'. Causative stem of badal. The same root returns for the firmament (1:6, 7) and the lights (1:14, 18); it is the chapter's main creative verb after 'say'.
'Good': suited to its purpose, well-working, not only morally good.

verses.translation_literal: And-called God to-the-light Day, and-to-the-darkness he-called Night. And-was evening and-was morning, day one.
verses.translation_dramatic: God named the light Day, and the darkness he named Night. Evening came, and morning came: one day.
verses.directors_commentary:
In the ancient Near East, to name a thing is to claim authority over it, as a king names a conquered city. God names day and night and so they belong to him. Say the names with the calm of ownership.

The last line is the one the KJV changes. 'The evening and the morning were the first day' reads as an ordinal with an article. The Hebrew has no article and a cardinal number: yom echad, 'day one'. Every other day gets an ordinal (second, third) and the word choice here is odd enough to be remarked upon. The count also runs from evening to morning, which is the Israelite day: it begins at sunset, as the Sabbath still does. Dark comes first, then light, a pattern the audience would feel as a promise.

philological_notes.note: 'Day one', with a cardinal number, where days 2 to 6 use ordinals. Often rendered 'the first day', but the Hebrew form is a plain count.
'He called, named'. Naming expresses authority. Here the verb appears twice, with a wordplay of light-day, dark-night.

verses.translation_literal: And-said God: Let-be an-expanse in-the-midst-of the-waters, and-let-it-be separating between waters to-waters.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God said, "Let there be a vault in the midst of the waters, and let it stand dividing water from water."
verses.directors_commentary:
The command now asks for space. Water is everywhere, and God makes a gap in the middle of it. The actor should speak the word 'vault' as if shaping it with the hands.

The KJV's 'firmament' comes through the Latin firmamentum, from the Greek stereoma, 'a solid structure'. The Hebrew raqia' comes from the verb raqa', 'to beat out, to stretch', used of beaten metal plates (Num 17:3 in the Hebrew numbering; Radak cites it). Ibn Ezra reads it as something stretched out, like a tent, and Radak as the air surrounding the globe, so the word's picture is of a thing hammered or spread thin. The sky is usually understood as a dome or vault holding water above and below, and BBE's 'solid arch' leans that way; YLT's 'expanse' avoids the question rather than settling it. The commentators in the packet differ on how solid it is, and the verse does not say.

Also easy to miss: the participle mavdil, 'separating', is a continuous action, not a one-time event. The firmament is told to be a divider, not only to divide, and Radak makes the point that here the vault is the one that separates, unlike the light and darkness of verse 4, where God does. And 'between waters to waters' puts the word mayim in two forms side by side, a visible echo.

philological_notes.note: From raqa', 'beat out, stretch'. Radak calls anything stretched or beaten out a raqia', citing the beaten plates of Num 17:3, and takes it here as the air around the earth. Ibn Ezra compares stretching a tent. The Latin 'firmamentum' (KJV 'firmament') carries an idea of solidity that the Hebrew root does not itself require.
A participle: 'a separator', a standing function, not a single act.

verses.translation_literal: And-made God [obj] the-expanse, and-separated between the-waters which [were] beneath the-expanse and-between the-waters which [were] above the-expanse. And-it-was so.
verses.translation_dramatic: So God made the vault, and set it between the waters: the waters beneath it, and the waters above it. And so it was.
verses.directors_commentary:
The command is carried out in the next breath, and the camera lingers on the geometry: under, above, and the divider in between. Play it as a measured, almost architectural sentence.

Note that the verb changes. Verse 6 had God 'say', and here God 'makes' (vayya'as) the vault, a plain verb of making beside the verbs of speech; the KJV renders it faithfully, but a reader should notice that word and deed now stand side by side. 'And it was so' (vayehi khen) is a stock closing formula, the Hebrew equivalent of 'done', and it recurs through the chapter. The ancient picture is of upper waters, the source of rain, held back by the vault. Rain was a sensitive subject in lands without a dependable river; the audience knows who controls it.

philological_notes.note: 'And it was so': the formula that confirms a command carried out, repeated through the chapter.

verses.translation_literal: And-called God to-the-expanse Heavens. And-was evening and-was morning, day second.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God named the vault Heavens. Evening came, and morning came: a second day.
verses.directors_commentary:
A quiet closing beat. The vault is named, and the name, shamayim, is the same word as the 'heavens' of verse 1: the first verse is now filled in. Let the actor mark the connection.

Two things the KJV conceals. First, shamayim is a plural-looking form, so 'Heaven' is too singular, and the KJV's capital letter makes it a place name. Second, this is the only day in the Hebrew text without 'and God saw that it was good'. The Septuagint adds it; the Hebrew does not, and the usual explanations (the waters are not yet finished, since they are gathered on day three) are guesses. The actor can use the silence. The count here is ordinal, 'day second', as against 'day one' in verse 5.

philological_notes.note: 'Heavens': a plural or dual-looking form, always plural in Hebrew. The vault takes the name already used in 1:1.

verses.translation_literal: And-said God: Let-be-gathered the-waters from-under the-heavens to place one, and-let-appear the-dry-ground. And-it-was so.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God said, "Let the waters beneath the heavens gather into one place, and let the dry ground be seen." And so it was.
verses.directors_commentary:
The waters are told to move, and the land is not made but revealed. Note that the verb is 'let it appear', a word of seeing: the dry ground was there beneath the water and now comes into view. Play the second half as an unveiling.

The KJV's 'dry land' is accurate; yabbashah is 'the dry', the dry thing, a word from the same root as dried-up riverbeds, and for an audience of farmers it means the ground that can bear a crop. The KJV's 'gathered together unto one place' hides the verb yiqqavu, which is a pun on miqveh, 'collection', in the next verse. And 'one place' is a poetic singular: the sea is pictured as a single great basin ringed by land, as the Israelites knew from the coast.

philological_notes.note: 'Let them be gathered' (niphal). The root also gives miqveh, 'a gathering', in 1:10.
'The dry (thing)', the dry ground, used for land as opposed to sea.

verses.translation_literal: And-called God to-the-dry-ground Earth, and-to-the-gathering-of the-waters he-called Seas. And-saw God that [it was] good.
verses.translation_dramatic: God named the dry ground Earth, and the gathered waters he named Seas. And God saw that it was good.
verses.directors_commentary:
Naming again, and again the sign of rule. The land becomes 'Earth' (eretz), the same word as in verse 1, and the waters, now penned in, get a plural name: yammim, 'seas'. Give the naming the same calm as in verse 5, and let the verdict land softly.

The KJV's 'gathering together of the waters called he Seas' is faithful, and the word order in Hebrew is also reversed for emphasis ('and to the gathering of the waters he called'), which the KJV keeps. What it misses is the sound of it: miqveh and yiqqavu are the same root, so the waters are 'gathered' into a 'gathering'. The sea in the surrounding cultures is a god or a monster; here it is a named, contained body of water that God calls good.

philological_notes.note: 'A gathering, a collection', formed from the same root as the verb yiqqavu in 1:9, a deliberate echo.
'Seas', plural. The named waters include all the bodies of water, not one sea.

verses.translation_literal: And-said God: Let-sprout the-earth sprouts, plants seed-bearing seed, trees-of fruit making fruit to-its-kind, which its-seed [is] in-it upon the-earth. And-it-was so.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God said, "Let the earth sprout green: plants bearing seed, and trees bearing fruit, each after its kind, with its seed within it, upon the earth." And so it was.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the earth itself is addressed, and given a job. The command is almost a pun: tadshe' ha'arets deshe', 'let the earth sprout sprouts'. Let the actor play with the repetition, and imagine the first green showing at the edge of bare ground.

The KJV's 'grass' is misleading. Deshe' is not only lawn: it is the fresh green growth of the land, the first tender shoots, and the verse then sorts it into two kinds of food plant: seed-bearing herbs (the grain of the farmer) and fruit trees. Both are defined by their seed, which is in them. The KJV's 'after his kind' is only a matter of English pronouns: Hebrew has no neuter, so lemino ('to its kind') carries a masculine suffix, and modern English says 'its'. The word min, 'kind', gives the ancient classification of plants and animals into their types, which for a farmer means that wheat gives wheat. Notice also the order, and what is missing: no sun yet, and the plants arrive by decree of the God who addresses the earth. Some read this as set against the fertility gods of Canaan, who were thought to give the grain; the verse does not say so, but a farming audience would hear who gives the harvest.

philological_notes.note: A verb and its own noun together: 'let the earth sprout sprouts'. It is a cognate accusative, and deshe' means tender green growth, not only grass. This is my own reading of the construction.
'To its kind'. Min is the category into which living things are sorted; the same word recurs for the animals.

verses.translation_literal: And-brought-out the-earth sprouts, plants seed-bearing seed to-its-kind, and-trees making fruit which its-seed [was] in-it to-its-kind. And-saw God that [it was] good.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the earth brought forth: green shoots, and plants bearing seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit with the seed inside, each after its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verses.directors_commentary:
The earth obeys, and the verse is nearly the command played back, with small changes. Let the actor hear that it is the earth that acts: va-totse ha'arets, 'and the earth brought out'. There is a modest, almost proud tone in the report.

The KJV gives 'brought forth grass' again, with the same flattening of deshe' that it made in verse 11. The Hebrew also says 'to its kind' three times where the English ('after his kind' twice) is shorter, and the order of the two plant types is slightly rearranged; the effect is a measured, orderly repetition. The verdict 'good' now follows a creative act of the earth itself. Day three carries two verdicts of 'good' (verses 10 and 12), one for the land and sea and one for the crop: a detail the farmer in the audience will understand, since land and harvest are two gifts.

philological_notes.note: 'And it brought out'. The earth is the subject, as the command in 1:11 asked.

verses.translation_literal: And there was evening and there was morning, day third.
verses.translation_dramatic: Evening came, and the light went out of the green hills. And morning came, and the light returned to them. A third day.
verses.directors_commentary:
The refrain is the same as before, and it is meant to be heard as a refrain: the same six words, the same weight, a door closing on one day and opening on the next. Say it plainly. The pattern runs evening first, then morning, which is how an ancient listener counted a day: it begins when the light fails, not when it returns.

The KJV reads 'And the evening and the morning were the third day', and that is a small harmonizing change. Hebrew has no 'the' on evening or morning and says twice, 'there was', once for each. The ordinal 'third' stands without the article: 'day third', not 'the third day'. The same bare ordinal appears on days two to five, while day one is the cardinal 'one day' (1:5) and day six alone takes the article, 'the sixth day' (1:31). So the KJV's 'the' flattens a pattern. Whether it is deliberate is for the reader to judge, but the Hebrew keeps the days as a counted sequence, not a set of named, definite days until the last one.

philological_notes.note: 'Day third', with no article on the ordinal. This is the pattern for days two to five; day one is the cardinal 'yom echad' (1:5) and day six has the article (1:31). The article-less ordinal presents each day as one more in a count.

verses.translation_literal: And God said, Let there be luminaries in the firmament of the heavens to separate between the day and between the night, and they shall be for signs and for appointed times and for days and years.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God spoke again into the dark: Let there be lamps hung in the vault of the heavens. Let them stand guard over the border between day and night, and let them be signs to read, and appointed times to keep, and a count of days and of years.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the longest command so far, and its length is its content: the speaker is handing out jobs. Four of them are listed after 'to separate': signs, appointed times, days, years. Play it as a briefing, not a flash of power.

The KJV's 'lights' loses a distinction the Hebrew makes. These are מְאֹרֹת, 'luminaries', bearers or holders of light, and not the 'or', light itself, that God called into being on day one (1:3). The light was already there; what is made now are the things that carry it. Rashi and Radak, in the packet, both hold that the luminaries existed from the first day and were only set in the sky on the fourth (Rashi on Genesis 1:14; Radak on Genesis 1:14); the verb here is a command, 'let there be', and the Hebrew does not itself decide that question. The KJV's 'firmament of the heaven' also turns a plural, 'the heavens', into a singular.

The KJV's 'seasons' for מוֹעֲדִים is the most important softening. The word means 'appointed times', fixed meetings, and is the word for the festivals and for the 'tent of meeting'. Ramban reads it as sowing, harvest, cold and heat (Ramban on Genesis 1:14), and Rashi as the festivals Israel would later be commanded to keep (Rashi on Genesis 1:14). Either way the heavens here are a calendar kept by appointment, not just weather. 'Signs' are omens as well as markers: Rashi and Ramban both link it to Jeremiah 10:2, 'signs of the heavens'.

Notice the verb 'to separate', לְהַבְדִּיל, the same verb used for light and dark on day one (1:4). The first separation was done by God directly; now it is handed to the sky. Notice, too, that the sun and the moon are never named; the text says only 'luminaries'. A common modern reading is that this avoids the names that were also the names of gods in neighbouring cultures, but none of the commentaries in the packet gives that reason, and it should be treated as an interpretation. A small grammatical point, from Radak: the verb 'let there be' is singular although 'luminaries' is plural (Radak on Genesis 1:14).

philological_notes.note: 'Luminaries', light-bearers: a derived noun with the instrument prefix, distinct from אוֹר, light itself (1:3). Rashi notes the word is written defectively, without the vav, and draws a lesson from the similarity to מְאֵרָה, 'curse'; that is a homiletic reading, not a claim about the original meaning.

'And for appointed times': fixed meetings, festivals. The KJV 'seasons' is too weak, since the word is the one used for sacred assemblies and the tent of meeting. Rashi connects it to the festivals Israel would be commanded to keep; Ramban to the agricultural seasons.
'For signs': markers, and also omens, as in Jeremiah 10:2, 'signs of the heavens'. Ibn Ezra and Ramban both quote that verse here.

verses.translation_literal: And they shall be for luminaries in the firmament of the heavens to give light upon the earth. And it was so.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them hang as lamps in the arch of the heavens, and pour their light down on the earth. And so it was.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the second half of the commission, now said for its own sake: the luminaries are not decoration for the sky but light for the earth below. The last three words, 'and it was so', are the sentence of fulfilment; speak them flat and quick, with no boasting, because in this chapter the word and the deed are one. The KJV has 'And let them be for lights', with a 'let' that the Hebrew does not have: the verb is a plain future, 'and they shall be', the same form as the end of the previous verse. Radak and Ramban read this verse as adding that their light actually reaches the earth, not merely shines in the sky.

philological_notes.note: 'To give light', a causative infinitive: the luminaries are the ones who make light fall on something else. The same root as 'luminaries' (me'orot) and 'light' (or), so the sentence is an echo of itself in Hebrew.

verses.translation_literal: And God made the two luminaries, the great ones: the luminary, the great, for the dominion of the day, and the luminary, the small, for the dominion of the night, and the stars.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God made them: the two great lamps. The greater lamp, to hold dominion over the day; the lesser lamp, to hold dominion over the night. And the stars.
verses.directors_commentary: Here at last the two bodies appear, and still the text will not say 'sun' or 'moon': they are 'the great luminary' and 'the small luminary', and the rule they hold is a delegated one, a mem-shelet, 'dominion', the same word family as the later rule of kings. The stars come in at the very end, three words with no ceremony; the KJV's 'he made the stars also' puffs this into an afterthought with an added 'also', where the Hebrew simply says 'and the stars', leaving the actress to decide how casual to make it. Where polytheistic neighbours worshipped these bodies, the text makes them lamps on a chain of command, and makes the stars almost an aside. 'Great' is not size: Radak and Ibn Ezra, who knew that other planets are larger than the moon, say it means great in light. Note that the Hebrew has the verb 'made' (asah), not 'created'; the Hebrew bara is saved for the sea monsters in verse 21.

philological_notes.note: 'For the dominion of': a noun for the exercise of rule, not just a verb 'to rule'. Radak reads it as the working effect of the lights, not just their shining.
'The great ones.' Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as great in light, not in body, since other planets are larger than the moon; Ibn Ezra compares Jesse's 'great' sons, great relative to the others.

verses.translation_literal: And God set them in the firmament of the heavens to give light upon the earth,
verses.translation_dramatic: And God set them there, fixed in the arch of the heavens, to pour their light down upon the earth,
verses.directors_commentary: 'Set' is the verb of placement, nathan, 'to give, to put': God does not just make the lamps, he puts each one where it belongs, like a craftsman hanging them in a ceiling. Radak notes that the two verbs 'made' and 'set' are distinct: the first says what they are, the second says that on this day they were placed in the sky. The line is calm and even, a pause between the list of duties and the verdict; let the voice stay low. KJV 'set' is accurate here; the BBE 'put' is closer to the plain word.

philological_notes.note: 'And he set/gave/placed.' Ibn Ezra defends the use of 'give' for placement by pointing to God's setting of the rainbow in the cloud in Genesis 9:13.

verses.translation_literal: And to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate between the light and between the darkness. And God saw that [it was] good.
verses.translation_dramatic: To rule the day and to rule the night, and to hold the light and the darkness apart. And God looked, and it was good.
verses.directors_commentary: The long sentence of duties that began at verse 14 ends here, and with it the verdict that closes each stage: 'God saw that it was good'. 'Good' is tov, which means fit for its purpose, well made, as much as it means morally good; the actor should play satisfaction at a job well done, not sentiment. KJV 'divide the light from the darkness' keeps the word 'divide' from verse 14 but moves it from 'day and night' to 'light and darkness': Ramban and Ibn Ezra argue over whether these are the same pair. The word 'rule' here is the plain verb mashal, used for kings and governors; the sun and moon have been given an office. Ancient listeners also knew the 'rule' of the heavenly bodies as astral power, which Ramban discusses; the text itself says only that they rule day and night.

philological_notes.note: 'And to rule', infinitive of the verb behind 'dominion' in verse 16. Ramban takes the rule as more than lighting: the lights also govern the growth and change of earthly things.
'That [it was] good.' The repeated verdict of the chapter; tov is fitness for purpose as much as moral goodness.

verses.translation_literal: And there was evening and there was morning, day fourth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And evening fell, and morning broke. A fourth day.
verses.directors_commentary: The refrain again, and the shortest verse of the passage: let it be a breath, a hinge between the lamps in the sky and the first living things in the water. As with the other days the Hebrew reads 'day fourth' without an article, which the KJV turns into 'the fourth day'. Nothing is lost for a listener, but the Hebrew keeps the sense of a count still running.

verses.translation_literal: And God said, Let the waters swarm a swarming of living creatures, and let a bird fly above the earth on the face of the firmament of the heavens.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God spoke over the deep: Let the waters teem. Let them crowd with living, moving things; and let wings beat above the earth, across the face of the arching sky.
verses.directors_commentary: For the first time the command is for life, not for matter: nefesh chayah, a 'living creature', literally a living throat or breath. The word 'swarm' is doing the work: the Hebrew repeats the root sharats, 'let the waters swarm a swarm', and the actor should let the repeated sound crowd. The KJV 'bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life' says it differently and loses both the repetition and the order: the waters themselves are the subject, and they are told to teem. The KJV's 'open firmament' has no Hebrew behind 'open'; the phrase is 'on the face of the firmament', which puts the birds in front of the dome, flying across its visible surface, not under it. A hearer who lived under open sky would have seen it so: birds against the blue. Ramban and Radak note that the birds are mentioned here with the waters, because they too were said to arise from the waters.

philological_notes.note: 'Let them swarm a swarming.' The root means to teem or move in great numbers; Rashi limits sherets to creatures that stay close to the ground, while Onkelos and Radak take it as general movement and abundance.
'A living creature', literally 'a living soul/throat'. Rashi: that it has life; Ramban notes that plants are not called nefesh at all.

verses.translation_literal: And God created the great sea monsters, and every living creature that creeps, which the waters swarmed, to their kinds, and every winged bird to its kind. And God saw that [it was] good.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God created the great sea monsters, the vast dragons of the deep, and everything that lives and stirs, all that the waters had teemed with, each after its kind; and every bird of wing, each after its kind. And God looked, and it was good.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb here is bara, 'created', which the chapter has not used since its first verse and which always has God as its subject in the Bible; its object is the tanninim, the 'great sea monsters'. The KJV makes them 'great whales', which is neither accurate nor safe: tannin is elsewhere a serpent or dragon and appears in other Hebrew poetry as a figure of chaos; Ramban and Rashi connect it to Leviathan. In the neighbouring cultures the sea's monsters were gods or rivals of gods. Here they are listed first, with no struggle: created, named among the creatures, and called good. This is the voice to find: no awe of the monsters, just the declaration that they too were made. Note that, unlike the other days, the usual 'and it was so' is missing here, which Ramban and Radak both remark on. The phrase 'after its kind', 'to its kind', is in the Hebrew a preposition plus 'kind' (min), an order of species, not a mere comparison.

philological_notes.note: 'The sea monsters.' Rashi: large fish of the sea, and in the aggadah Leviathan and his mate. KJV 'whales' is a later narrowing.

'And he created.' Ramban says bara is used here because of the huge size of these creatures, to stress that God, not the waters, brought them into being; Radak says the waters lacked the power to bring forth life without God's help.
'That creeps / stirs.' Radak: 'that walks', its creeping being its swarming. Ibn Ezra mentions a view that the sin is a samekh.

verses.translation_literal: And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas, and let the bird multiply on the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God blessed them. He said: Bear young, and be many. Fill the waters of the seas; and let the birds be many on the earth.
verses.directors_commentary: The first blessing in the Bible, and it falls on animals: before humankind is made, God speaks directly to the creatures, 'saying'. Radak notes that the creatures cannot really hear; it is God's will in the form of a speech. The blessing is a gift of fertility, 'be fruitful and multiply', words the text will use again for the first human couple. The KJV 'fill the waters in the seas' is correct, but the shift to 'let fowl multiply' is a change of mood the Hebrew marks: the first three verbs are commands, the bird clause a jussive, 'let it multiply'. A good performance gives the first three verbs a ringing, rising force and then drops to a gentler wish for the birds. Rashi reads the blessing as needed because these creatures are hunted and eaten; the text itself does not say so.

philological_notes.note: 'And he blessed.' Ramban: a blessing here is fertility, the power to produce many of one's kind. Rashi connects the need for it to these creatures being hunted.
'Be fruitful and multiply.' Rashi: 'be fruitful' makes one produce one, and 'multiply' makes one produce many. Radak reads the imperative as an assurance of power, 'you shall bear'.

verses.translation_literal: And there was evening and there was morning, day fifth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And evening fell, and morning broke. A fifth day.
verses.directors_commentary: The refrain once more, now over a sea that is full and a sky that has wings in it. Keep it short and let the silence after it carry the water and the birds. As on every day but the last, the number has no article in the Hebrew: 'day fifth'. The KJV's 'the fifth day' fixes it as a known date.

verses.translation_literal: And God said, Let the earth bring forth living creatures to their kind: livestock and creeping things and the living things of the earth to their kind. And it was so.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God said: Let the earth bring forth the living, each after its kind, the tame herds, and the creeping things, and the wild beasts of the earth, each after its kind. And so it was.
verses.directors_commentary: The earth, which on day three was told to sprout plants, is now told to bring forth animals: the same verb, 'to bring out', the same earth, a deeper gift. Three kinds are named: behemah, the animals people keep and ride and eat, remesh, the creeping things, and chayto-eretz, 'the living things of the earth', which means wild animals, the ones that live outside human settlement. The KJV's 'cattle' is too narrow for behemah, and 'beast of the earth' for chayto-eretz hides the old ending -o on the construct form, an archaic spelling Ibn Ezra and Radak compare to 'son of Beor' in Numbers 24:3. For the first time the phrase 'after its kind' is used about land animals, and again for the second and third groups; the Hebrew is the same each time, so the repetition can be heard. The scene gives the audience a map of the ancient world: the animals of the farm, those that crawl, and the dangerous wild ones beyond the fields.

philological_notes.note: 'Livestock', the larger domestic animals. Ibn Ezra: animals that serve people for riding and food; Ramban: the grass-eating kinds, both settled and wild.
'Creeping things.' Rashi: low creatures that seem to drag themselves along so that their walking is not visible; Ibn Ezra: the small ones that go on the earth.
'And the living things of the earth', wild beasts. The final vav is an old genitive ending; Ibn Ezra and Radak compare 'son of Beor' (Num 24:3). Ramban: meat-eaters.

verses.translation_literal: And God made the living-thing of the earth to its kind, and the livestock to its kind, and every creeping-thing of the ground to its kind; and God saw that [it was] good.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God made them. The wild beasts of the earth, each after its kind; the tame herds, each after its kind; and every creeping thing that stirs along the ground, each after its kind. And God looked on what he had made, and saw that it was good.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as the quiet completion of the command in verse 24, not as a new speech. Verse 24 gave an order (livestock, creeping things, wild beasts); the doing in verse 25 reverses it, wild beasts first and creeping things last, so the verse closes on the smallest and lowest. The verb is 'made' (vayya'as), the workman's verb, after the earth was told to 'bring forth'; the earth supplies, God shapes. Rashi on this verse hears it as God fitting each creature out in its own beauty and stature.

The refrain 'to its kind' (lemino) is a built-in grammar lesson. It occurs three times: twice as lemina, with a feminine suffix, for the wild beast (chayyah) and the livestock (behemah), and once as lemineihu, with a masculine suffix, for the creeping thing (remes). Here the KJV muddies things. It writes 'after his kind' for the beast, then switches to 'their kind' for cattle, where the Hebrew is singular and has the same word both times; it also says the creeping thing 'creepeth upon the earth', but the Hebrew word is ha'adamah, 'the ground', the red soil Adam is named for, not 'ha'arets, the earth' used for the beast a moment before. The ground-creatures belong to the same dust as the human who is coming. Remes is a motion word, 'that which stirs low'; Radak on this verse notes it denotes movement, and has the creeping things dwelling in wild places, an interpretation of his, not a datum of the text.

There is no blessing here, unlike the sea creatures and birds in verse 22. Radak on this verse explains it by the danger of predators filling the earth; the text itself simply gives only the verdict 'good'. In an audience that knew the gods of Egypt and Canaan with animal forms, the quiet point is that lion, serpent and bull are creatures made by decree, not powers.

philological_notes.note: 'To its kind'. Twice lemina (feminine suffix, for chayyah and behemah), once lemineihu (masculine, for remes). The noun min, 'kind', is rare and used in the creation accounts to mark the fixed classes of living things; the KJV's mixture of 'his' and 'their' hides that each suffix agrees with the grammatical gender of its own noun.

'The living-thing of the earth', the wild land animals as opposed to the livestock. Radak on Genesis 1:25 takes it to mean predators such as the lion, bear, leopard and wolf, and compares Exodus 23:29, 'beast of the field'.

'Creeping thing of the ground'. The land is 'adamah here, not 'erets as in the first phrase; the word links these creatures with the 'adam made of the same soil. Radak on this verse glosses remes as a word of walking and movement.

verses.translation_literal: And God said: Let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness; and let them rule over the fish of the sea and over the bird of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth and over every creeper that creeps on the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God said: Let us make humankind, in our image, after our likeness. And let them rule over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the heavens, over the herds, over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps along it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The register changes here. Until now God has said 'let there be' and 'let the earth bring forth'; now he says 'let us make', in the first person plural and with a verb of making. Do not play it as a quarrel or a committee. The ancient commentators do not agree on who 'us' is: Rashi says God takes counsel with his heavenly court, to teach that the great should consult the small; Ramban and Radak (citing his father) read it as God addressing the earth, from which the body is drawn; Ibn Ezra, as the packet gives him, adds that kings speak in the plural. Whatever you decide, the sentence is a hinge, and everything before it was the stage.

The KJV 'Let us make man' hides something. It does keep the plural 'let them have dominion'. What 'man' obscures is that adam has no article here and is not a man: it is humankind, a collective, which is why the next verb is plural. Tselem, 'image', is a physical word (it is used for statues, as in the 'images of your tumors' of 1 Sam 6:5, noted by Radak), and a king's image stood for the king in the ancient Near East, so to be made in God's image is to stand for him in his world. 'Rule' is the plain sense of yirdu, and the rule extends to the fish and the birds, which Radak says can be governed only by craft since people do not live in the sea or the air. The KJV's 'fowl of the air' gives shamayim, 'the heavens', a thinner sense. The last phrase repeats the root remes ('every creeper that creeps'), which the KJV keeps with 'creeping thing that creepeth'. As for 'over all the earth' in the middle of a list of animals, Radak takes it to mean the wild animals; it may equally mean the land itself.

philological_notes.note: First person plural of 'make'. Rashi takes it as God consulting his court; Ramban and Radak take it as God and the earth together making the body; Ibn Ezra points to a king's plural. The text does not say.

'In our image'. Tzelem is a concrete word for a figure or a likeness. Radak sets the sense 'image' against 1 Sam 6:5 and Numbers 33:52, where it is a physical statue. The preposition be- is 'in'/'as'.
'And let them rule'. Rashi hears a second verb in it, yarad 'go down', and reads: if worthy, people rule the animals; if not, they sink below them. That is a homily, not the plain sense.

verses.translation_literal: And God created the human in his image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God created the human being in his own image. In the image of God he created him: male and female he created them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is built in three beats, almost like a verse of poetry: 'in his image / in the image of God / male and female'. The verb 'created' (bara) occurs three times in this one line. It is the verb reserved for God as its subject, and its triple use here marks the human as the climax of the sixth day.

Note the shift from singular to plural: 'created him' (oto), then 'created them' (otam). The collective human is one and also two. The KJV renders this smoothly as 'man ... him ... them', which keeps the grammar but flattens the effect. The phrase 'male and female' uses the plain biological words zakhar and nekevah, the same terms used for animals in the flood story; there is nothing delicate here, and the point is that both are in the image.

Rashi reads 'image' as the stamp of a seal on a coin: the human is pressed with a die, while everything else was made by speech. He also gives the older reading that the first human had two faces and was later divided, and the plain reading that both were made on the sixth day with the manner explained in chapter 2. Radak notes that the verb 'created' refers to the soul and chapter 2's 'formed' to the body. For a listener in the ancient world the surprise is that the 'image of God' is not a king or priest but every person.

philological_notes.note: 'He created.' The verb bara has only God as its subject in the Bible. Radak distinguishes it from 'formed' (yatsar) in chapter 2, saying creation here refers to the soul.
'Male and female': the ordinary terms for the sexes of animals and people. They are the same pair used for the animals in the flood story.
'In the image of God.' Rashi reads the image as a seal-stamp pressed on a coin; Radak says the image here is the mind or soul, like that of angels.

verses.translation_literal: And God blessed them, and God said to them: Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea and over the bird of the heavens and over every living-thing that creeps on the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God blessed them. And God said to them: Bear fruit, and multiply, and fill the earth, and bring it under you. Rule over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the heavens, and over every living thing that creeps upon the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the first time God speaks to the humans, not about them, and he begins with a blessing before the commands. Ramban notes that, unlike the blessing of the animals in verse 22, this one is followed by direct speech: 'and said to them'. Play the first three imperatives as a gift, not an order: be fruitful, multiply, fill. They are the same words God spoke to the fish and birds (v. 22), with fill extended from the seas to the earth. The KJV's 'replenish' is a trap for modern ears; in 1611 it meant 'fill', and mil'u says only 'fill'.

The second half is where the force lies, and the KJV is easy to misread. It keeps 'subdue it' for kivshuha, which is accurate: kavash is to bring under foot, to make subject, used of conquered land. What it softens is the next verb, radu, to 'have dominion', which sounds milder than the Hebrew 'rule'; the same root as in verse 26. The KJV also renders chayyah haromeset as 'every living thing that moveth', losing the repeated creeping root of 'creeps' and the fact that the phrase covers all land animals (Radak). In the ancient world this was a mandate for a farming people: to settle, clear, plant and herd, against the lion and the drought. Later Jewish tradition read the unusually spelled kivshuha as addressed to the man (Rashi, Radak on the missing vav), a legal reading, not the plain sense.

philological_notes.note: 'And subdue it'. The verb is used of bringing land under a conqueror. The spelling lacks the usual vav of the plural, which Rashi and Radak, following the Talmud, read as a singular addressed to the man.
'And rule'. The same verb as in verse 26. Ramban notes that the rabbis drew a distinction between kevishah (subduing) and rediyah (ruling); he takes redyah as the master's rule over his servant.
'Be fruitful and multiply'. Radak explains the first as begetting and the second as growing in number; the rabbis took it as a commandment on the man.

verses.translation_literal: And God said, 'Behold, I have given to you every seed-sowing plant which is on the face of all the earth, and every tree in which is tree-fruit sowing seed; to you it shall be for food.'
verses.translation_dramatic: And God said: Look. I have given you every plant on the face of all the earth that carries its seed, and every tree whose fruit holds seed within it. These shall be yours. These shall be your food.
verses.directors_commentary:
A grant of provision, in the legal language of a gift: hineh natatti lakhem, 'behold, I have given to you'. The perfect tense means the gift is already done. Radak compares it to a deed of sale, 'I have given the field' (Genesis 23:13). It is the first thing God hands over to the humans, and it is food from plants and trees, not meat.

That is the surprise for an ancient audience that ate meat at every sacrifice and feast. Ibn Ezra, Rashi, Ramban and Radak all read the verse to mean that meat was not permitted until after the flood (9:3), and Radak admits that he does not know why. The picture is of a world without killing at its start, in direct contrast to Mesopotamian myths where humans are made to feed the gods.

The KJV has 'herb bearing seed' and 'meat'. In 1611 'meat' meant food in general, but today it misleads in exactly the place where it matters, because the Hebrew okhlah means 'food' and the point is that there is no flesh in it. 'Herb' for esev also sounds like seasoning: it is the seed-bearing plants, which Ramban reads as the grains and legumes, with the tree-fruit as the second category.

The repeated phrase 'sowing seed' (zore'a zera) is a deliberate sound play: the plant and the fruit carry their own future. The harvest is built to be replanted. For farmers this is a promise of the cycle itself.

philological_notes.note: 'Sowing seed': a participle and its noun from the same root, said of both plant and tree. The sound play keeps the stress on the seed. Radak glosses it as 'causing seed to grow'.
'For food.' The word is the general term for eating. KJV 'meat' is an old English word for food in general, which today suggests flesh.

verses.translation_literal: And to every living-thing of the earth and to every bird of the heavens and to everything creeping on the earth, in which [is] a living nefesh, [I have given] all greenery of plant for food. And it was so.
verses.translation_dramatic: And to every wild creature of the earth, to every bird of the heavens, to everything that creeps on the ground, to all that has the breath of life in it, I have given the green of every plant to eat. And it was so.
verses.directors_commentary:
God is still speaking; this is the second half of one sentence that began in verse 29, and the verb 'I have given' is not repeated. Speak it as one breath, so that the animals are fed in the same sentence as the humans. The surprise is for the modern ear: in this first world nobody eats flesh. Humans receive seed-bearing plants and fruit trees; the animals receive the green growth. Ramban, on verse 29, reads this as a deliberate limit that stands until Noah; Radak observes that it includes even the lions.

The KJV renders nefesh chayyah as 'wherein there is life', which loses the word nefesh, the living being, the same term used for the animals at the beginning of the day and for the man in Genesis 2:7. Its 'green herb' is fine, but yerek 'esev is more exactly 'the green of plants', a phrase of freshness: what grows green is the animals' table, and the human table is seed and fruit. The closing 'and it was so' appears after most of the commands of the six days, but it is missing on day five, where the fish and birds are blessed instead; here it seals the gift of food.

philological_notes.note: 'A living being', the term for a creature that breathes. In Genesis 1 it names the animals; the KJV's 'life' drops the word nefesh. Radak says whatever has a nefesh chayyah ranks above a plant, which has only a growing nature, and the lower is made for the higher.

'Green of plants', that is fresh vegetation. Radak says yerek is attached to 'esev because a plant is eaten mostly while it is still green. Sforno separates it from the seed-bearing plants given to humans.

verses.translation_literal: And God saw all that he had made, and behold, [it was] good, very. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God looked upon everything he had made, and there it was: good. Very good. And there was evening, and there was morning: the sixth day.
verses.directors_commentary:
The refrain has been 'God saw that it was good' six times. Here it changes in three ways: God sees 'all that he had made', not one thing; the word 'behold' (hineh) is added, which makes the reader see it with him; and 'good' becomes 'very good' (tov me'od). The pause before 'very' is the high point of the whole chapter.

The KJV 'very good' is accurate, but the Hebrew order is 'good, very', and the listener hears the weight of the second word. Ramban reads 'very' as pointing to the whole order of things, including what looks like harm; the Midrash he and Radak cite plays on me'od ('very') and mot ('death'): the rabbis taught that 'very good' includes death, the evil impulse and suffering, because without them nothing would be built or begun. These are rabbinic readings, not what the plain text says, and an actor does not need them to play the verse.

The closing formula is also different. Days one to five had no article: 'a second day', 'a third day'. Here it is 'the sixth day' (yom hashishi), with the definite article. Radak says the article marks the day as the known day on which the world was completed; Rashi takes it as the sixth of Sivan, the day Torah was given. The KJV also writes 'the evening and the morning were the sixth day', which turns the Hebrew's two separate clauses 'and there was evening, and there was morning' into one. Evening comes first because the Hebrew day begins at sunset.

philological_notes.note: 'Good, very.' The word me'od, 'very', is new in the refrain. Ramban reads it as the goodness of the whole ordered world. Radak cites the midrash that plays on me'od and mot (death).

'The sixth day', with the definite article, which the first five days lack. Radak reads it as the known day on which the world was complete; Ibn Ezra says it means only the sixth in counting from the first day.

events.title: God creates the heavens and the earth
events.narrative_summary: In the beginning God creates the heavens and the earth. The earth is formless and empty, darkness lies over the deep, and the spirit of God hovers over the waters.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 1:1–2 stands before the first counted day, so it is placed at anchor.creation (Anno Mundi 1) itself with no duration. 'In the beginning' gives no number, hence MACRO_ERA. Rashi and the YLT read 1:1 as a clause leading into 1:2–3; I keep it as a scene of its own.

events.title: God makes light and separates it from darkness
events.narrative_summary: God says 'Let there be light', and there is light. He separates light from darkness and names them Day and Night; there is evening and morning, day one.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Anchored on the end of the opening scene, with time_of_day EREV because the Hebrew day counts from the evening ('there was evening and there was morning', 1:5): it starts at 18:00 on the creation date and lasts 24 hours. Dates are midnight to midnight, so the day shown covers two calendar dates. Rashi on 1:5 notes 'day one' rather than 'first day'; Ramban/Ibn Ezra read it as the turning of the sphere. No offset: the text gives no gap.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: There was evening and there was morning, day one

events.title: God makes the firmament and calls it Heaven
events.narrative_summary: God makes an expanse in the midst of the waters, dividing the waters below it from those above, and calls it Heaven. There is evening and morning, a second day.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts the moment day one ends (END, no offset), as the evening-and-morning formula of 1:5 closes day one and 1:8 closes this one; 24 hours.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: There was evening and there was morning, a second day

events.title: The waters gather and dry land appears
events.narrative_summary: God commands the waters under the heavens to gather into one place so that dry ground shows, and it is so. He names the dry ground Earth and the gathered waters Seas, and sees that it is good.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A child of day three, anchored on its START with no offset since the day opens with this act; about six hours is my estimate and the 12-hour margin shows that the text gives no length.

events.title: God gathers the waters and the earth sprouts plants
events.narrative_summary: On the third day God gathers the waters so the dry ground appears, names land and seas, and has the earth bring forth plants and fruit trees. There is evening and morning, a third day.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts when day two ends; 24 hours covering 1:9–13. Its two acts are children below.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: There was evening and there was morning, a third day

events.title: The earth brings forth plants and fruit trees
events.narrative_summary: God commands the earth to sprout vegetation, seed-bearing plants and fruit trees after their kinds, and the earth brings them forth. God sees that it is good.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the gathering of the waters within the same day (1:9–12 are consecutive speeches with no gap), so it is anchored on that event's END; six hours is an estimate, margin 12 hours.

events.title: God sets the sun, moon and stars in the sky
events.narrative_summary: God makes lights in the firmament to divide day from night and to serve as signs, seasons, days and years. He makes the greater light for the day, the lesser for the night, and the stars, and sets them in the sky. There is evening and morning, a fourth day.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts when day three ends; 24 hours (1:14–19). Radak and Ramban discuss how the first light relates to the luminaries; the dating is unaffected.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: There was evening and there was morning, a fourth day

events.title: God fills the waters and the sky with life
events.narrative_summary: God creates the great sea creatures, every living creature that swarms in the waters, and every winged bird, and blesses them to be fruitful and multiply. There is evening and morning, a fifth day.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts when day four ends; 24 hours (1:20–23).
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: There was evening and there was morning, a fifth day

events.title: God makes the land animals
events.narrative_summary: God commands the earth to bring forth living creatures, cattle, creeping things and wild animals after their kinds, and makes them. He sees that it is good.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Opens day six, so anchored on the parent's START with no offset; about six hours is an estimate, margin 12 hours.

events.title: God makes the land animals and humankind
events.narrative_summary: On the sixth day God makes the land animals, creates humankind male and female in his image, gives plants as food, and sees that all he has made is very good. There is evening and morning, the sixth day.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts when day five ends; 24 hours (1:24–31). Its four beats are children below.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: There was evening and there was morning, the sixth day

events.title: God creates humankind in his image
events.narrative_summary: God says 'Let us make humankind in our image' to rule over the animals, and creates them male and female. He blesses them and tells them to be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, subdue it and rule over the creatures.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the animals (1:24–25) in the same day; the decision, creation and blessing are continuous and form one event. Six hours is an estimate with a 6-hour margin.

events.title: God gives plants as food to humans and animals
events.narrative_summary: God says he has given every seed-bearing plant and every fruit tree to humankind for food, and every green plant to the animals, birds and creeping things, and it is so.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A speech of minutes, set after the blessing of 1:28 because it is addressed to those just created; one hour allowed, margin 3 hours.

events.title: God sees that all he made is very good
events.narrative_summary: God looks at everything he has made and sees that it is very good, and the sixth day closes.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The verdict of 1:31 comes after all the works of the day. Radak on 1:31, citing Bereshit Rabbah 9:14, says the work of the world was completed in the extra hour at the close of the sixth day, so it is the last hour of the 24-hour day: anchored on the day's START with offset 23 hours (the schema allows no negative offset, so this equals the day's END minus one hour), duration 1 hour, so it ends with the day. The 3-hour margin covers the gap after the food speech.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: There was evening and there was morning, the sixth day

causal_edges.causal_explanation: The firmament separated the waters below from those above, leaving the waters under the heavens to be gathered into one place (1:7, 1:9).
The plants and fruit trees the earth brought forth on day three are what God gives as food on day six (1:11–12, 1:29–30).
God's gift of food is addressed to the humans just created (1:27–29).
The dominion given to humankind covers the land animals and creeping things, which already exist (1:24–26).

entities.etymology_meaning: Maor means a light-bearer or luminary; gadol means great.
entities.summary_bio: The greater of two luminaries God makes on the fourth day and sets in the firmament to rule the day. The text does not call it the sun.

entities.etymology_meaning: Maor means a light-bearer or luminary; qatan means small.
entities.summary_bio: The smaller of two luminaries God makes on the fourth day and sets in the firmament to rule the night, together with the stars. The text does not call it the moon.

entities.etymology_meaning: Of means flying creature or bird; ha-shamayim, 'of the heavens', places it in the sky.
entities.summary_bio: The winged creatures of the sky, created and blessed on the fifth day together with the creatures of the waters. Humankind is to rule over them, and God gives them the green plants for food.

entities.etymology_meaning: Adam is probably tied to adamah, 'ground', which would make it 'the earthling'; here it is a collective noun for male and female.
entities.summary_bio: Humankind is made on the sixth day in God's image and likeness, male and female. God blesses them, commands them to be fruitful, to fill and subdue the earth and to rule the animals, and gives them plants for food.

entities.etymology_meaning: Chayyat ha-aretz means 'living creature of the earth'; behemah is livestock and remes the creeping things.
entities.summary_bio: The animals of the dry land in three kinds: wild beasts, livestock and creeping things. God makes them on the sixth day at his word to the earth and later gives them green plants for food.

aliases: the sea monsters and every living creature of the waters
entities.etymology_meaning: Sherets, 'swarming things', is the verb used of the waters teeming with life (1:20-21).
entities.summary_bio: The living creatures of the waters and the winged birds of the sky, made on the fifth day. God blesses them to be fruitful, multiply and fill the seas and the earth.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew eretz means earth, land or ground; at 1:10 God names the dry ground 'Earth'.
entities.summary_bio: The earth is created at the beginning together with the heavens. It is first formless and empty under darkness and water, and then takes shape as dry land, bears plants and is filled with animals and humankind.

entities.etymology_meaning: Shamayim is a dual or plural form meaning 'heavens'; raqia, the firmament, probably means a beaten-out expanse.
entities.summary_bio: The heavens are created with the earth in 1:1. On the second day God makes the firmament between the waters and calls it Heaven. The luminaries are set in it on the fourth day.

entities.etymology_meaning: Yammim is the plural of yam, 'sea'; the name is given at 1:10 to the gathering of the waters.
entities.summary_bio: On the third day God gathers the waters under the heavens into one place so that dry land can appear, and calls the gathered waters Seas. On the fifth day sea creatures fill them.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew choshekh means darkness; God names it Night (laylah) at 1:5.
entities.summary_bio: Darkness covers the deep before God speaks. God separates the light from it and calls it Night.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew or means light; God names it Day (yom) at 1:5.
entities.summary_bio: Light is the first thing God calls into being by speaking, on the first day. God sees that it is good, separates it from the darkness and calls it Day.

components.evidence_explanation: GEN.1.2: the earth was 'tohu wa-bohu', with darkness on the face of the deep.
GEN.1.9-10: the waters are gathered and the dry land is named Earth. The label is an inference from the text.
GEN.1.16: the greater luminary is made 'for the rule of the day'.
GEN.1.27: God created humankind in his own image, male and female.
GEN.1.28: God commands them to rule the fish, the birds and every living thing on the earth.
GEN.1.16: the lesser luminary is made 'for the rule of the night'.

systems.name: Creation by divine word
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Neighbouring cosmologies describe the world's making through combat with chaos (Enuma Elish) or through the speech of a god (Memphite Theology of Ptah). Genesis 1 presents the one God shaping chaos by command, without struggle.
rules_and_mechanics: God speaks a command ('Let there be...').
The result is reported at once: 'and it was so'.
God sees that the result is good.
Each day, not each act, is closed by 'evening and morning'.
The verb bara (create) has only God as its subject; asah (make) is also used of the earth bringing forth.

systems.name: Divine blessing of fertility
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Fertility of the land, the herds and the family was the chief concern of ancient Near Eastern blessings, and gods were asked to grant it. Genesis 1 gives it as a gift of the one Creator.
rules_and_mechanics: God speaks the blessing directly to those blessed.
The content is 'be fruitful and multiply and fill'.
The blessing is given to living creatures, and to humankind with the added command to subdue and rule.

systems.name: Divine naming
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Naming something in the ancient Near East signified knowing it, defining its role and holding authority over it. 'When above, the heavens had not been named' opens Enuma Elish.
rules_and_mechanics: The one who names has authority over what is named.
God calls (qara) a thing by a name.
The name states the thing's role: day, night, heaven, earth, seas.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God calls the light Day and the darkness Night.
system_instances.significance_note: Naming marks the divide of time and the Creator's authority over it.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The waters gather into one place and the dry ground appears.
system_instances.significance_note: It prepares the ground for plants, animals and humankind.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God calls the dry ground Earth and the gathered waters Seas.
system_instances.significance_note: The two names set the world's basic order of land and sea.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God makes a firmament in the midst of the waters, dividing the waters below from the waters above.
system_instances.significance_note: It forms the space in which the world is set.
The name states its role as the sky over the earth.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God blesses humankind: be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, subdue it and rule over the animals.
system_instances.significance_note: It sets out humankind's place and task in the created order.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God says 'Let us make humankind in our image' and creates them male and female.
system_instances.significance_note: The high point of the chapter: humankind alone is said to bear God's image.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The earth produces and God makes wild beasts, livestock and creeping things after their kinds.
system_instances.significance_note: It completes the living creatures before humankind.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God says 'Let there be light' and light comes to be.
system_instances.significance_note: The first act of making in the chapter, done by speech alone, which sets the pattern for the days that follow.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God makes two great luminaries and the stars and sets them in the firmament.
system_instances.significance_note: They give light, divide day from night and mark signs, seasons, days and years.

system_instances.outcome_summary: At God's word the earth brings forth plants and fruit trees, each after its kind.
system_instances.significance_note: The earth is the means of production here, and the plants are later given as food (1:29).

system_instances.outcome_summary: God blesses them: be fruitful, multiply and fill the waters and the earth.
system_instances.significance_note: The first blessing in the Bible, and it concerns life that continues.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God creates the sea monsters, every swarming creature of the waters and every winged bird.
system_instances.significance_note: The first living creatures; the verb bara is used again, as in 1:1.

God blesses the creatures of the waters and the birds to be fruitful and multiply.

God creates humankind in his image, male and female.
God commands light into being on the first day.
God commands the waters under the heavens to gather into one place.
God gives the animals and birds the green plants for food.
God gives the birds of the heavens the green plants for food.
God gives humankind every seed-bearing plant and every fruit tree for food.

God makes the greater luminary to rule the day.
God makes the land animals, each after its kind.
God makes the lesser luminary to rule the night.
God divides the light from the darkness.
